Northern studfish (Fundulus catenatus) exhibits considerable sexual size dimorphism, a trait documented across several field surveys in the eastern and central United States. Females in most populations achieve an asymptotic body size of 9.5 centimeters [Li = 9.5 centimeters] in total length, whereas males grow substantially larger and reach an ultimate total length of 16 centimeters [Li = 16 centimeters]. This disparity in maximum size likely reflects differential selective pressures related to reproductive tactics, with larger males gaining advantages in territorial defense and courtship displays. Mark-recapture studies conducted in Kentucky and Tennessee streams have confirmed that this species can live for a considerable duration under ambient thermal regimes. In captivity, however, conditions are often standardized for comparative physiology. At a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for the northern studfish is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], a longevity that is moderate among topminnows but exceeds that of several smaller fundulid congeners. This duration allows for multiple reproductive seasons over an individual's lifetime.

Puberty in Fundulus catenatus is reached after a relatively brief juvenile period when compared to its ultimate lifespan. Laboratory-reared individuals maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] attain sexual maturity at approximately 2 years after hatching [tp = approximately 2 years after hatching], a pace that aligns with the species' life history as a periodic strategist in stable headwater environments. The standard length at which this developmental milestone is achieved has been estimated at 3.8 centimeters [Lp = 3.8 centimeters], a figure derived from morphometric comparisons with the related species Fundulus dispar. This body size at puberty represents a substantial proportion of the female ultimate length, suggesting that a significant degree of somatic growth must occur before the onset of gonadal recrudescence. Field collections have corroborated this laboratory finding, as gravid females captured from the Barren River system rarely measure less than four centimeters in standard length. The timing of maturation appears to be influenced by local thermal regimes, with southern populations potentially reaching maturity slightly earlier than those at higher latitudes.

Neonatal mass in Fundulus catenatus is remarkably low, reflecting the species' reproductive mode of producing small, demersal eggs. The wet weight at birth has been estimated at approximately 0.0092 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0092 grams], a value derived from egg diameter measurements in the congener Fundulus parvipinnis and adjusted for the relative size of the northern studfish. These tiny yolk-sac larvae, often termed prolarvae or sac-fry, measure only a few millimeters upon eclosion and rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days of exogenous feeding. The rapid absorption of the yolk sac coincides with the opening of the mouth gape, marking the trophic switch to active feeding on microzooplankton. This initial mass is minuscule compared to the juvenile and adult stages, highlighting the steep ontogenetic growth trajectory that characterizes the species. During the first summer, young-of-year individuals can increase their body weight by several orders of magnitude as they exploit rich invertebrate prey resources in shallow littoral zones.

Maximum reproductive output in Fundulus catenatus is tightly linked to the thermal conditions of the breeding season. Under laboratory conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females can achieve a remarkably high annual fecundity, producing an average of 245 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 245 eggs per nest], and are capable of completing approximately 0.67 nesting events per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.67 nesting events per day] during peak spawning periods. This translates into a daily reproduction rate that reflects an intense, short-lived reproductive burst characteristic of many topminnows. The extended nature of the spawning season, which can last several months in the wild, allows females to deposit numerous clutches across the spring and summer. Field studies in the Cumberland River drainage have documented gravid females with developing oocytes of multiple size classes, indicating batch spawning and the continuous recruitment of new oocytes. The high fecundity likely compensates for significant egg and larval mortality in the unpredictable stream environments they inhabit.

Adult body mass in Fundulus catenatus shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, consistent with the differences observed in total length. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 6.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 6.2 grams], whereas males, due to their greater length, attain a substantially higher ultimate wet weight of 30.8 grams [Wwi = 30.8 grams]. This nearly five-fold difference in mass is among the most extreme reported for the genus Fundulus and is associated with distinct ecological roles: larger males monopolize prime spawning territories among gravel substrates, while females allocate relatively more energy toward egg production. The relationship between length and weight follows a standard power function derived from large sample sizes, confirming that males grow in a heavier-bodied proportion than females. Dietary analyses suggest that this sexual divergence in size may be facilitated by males consuming larger benthic prey items, such as crayfish and large insect nymphs, whereas females focus on smaller invertebrates. This trophic partitioning likely reduces intraspecific competition and allows both sexes to co-occur at high densities in productive stream reaches.
